item.title: The Hip Hop Word Count: Blue Scholars Approved
item.dc:creator: Hollis
item.description: We wanted to let everyone know about this proposed project, The Hip Hop Word Count: A Searchable Rap Almanac, that takes being a hip-hop head to brainiac status. This guy Tahir Hemphill is the mastermind behind the project, which he describes thusly: How can analyzing lyrics teach us about our culture? The Hip-Hop Word Count [...]
item.content:encoded:
We wanted to let everyone know about this proposed project, The Hip Hop Word Count: A Searchable Rap Almanac, that takes being a hip-hop head to brainiac status. This guy Tahir Hemphill is the mastermind behind the project, which he describes thusly:

How can analyzing lyrics teach us about our culture?

The Hip-Hop Word Count locks in a time and geographic location for every metaphor, simile, cultural reference, phrase, meme and socio-political idea used in the corpus of Hip-Hop.

The Hip-Hop Word Count then converts this data into explorable visualisations which help us to comprehend this vast set of cultural data.

This data can be used to chart the migration of ideas and builds a geography of language and is the engine for a teaching curriculum.

As students, we learn that cultures are remembered and live on through how they’re documented, be it oral tradition, historical record, or otherwise. Hip-hop as a culture has its own documentation: its lyricism. Often times, academic takes on hip-hop forgo its own self-expression and context, with a anthropological, subjective and theory-heavy approach that zaps the authenticity out of the account. This is the genius of this project: a top-level, thorough and accessible platform to let rap lyrics– and hip-hop– speak for themselves, with infinite possibilities as to how it’s applied.

As of this writing, the project needs only $2,000 more to become reality. If you got the guap, consider donating to this project. And you might even get a cool, tasty Rap Chocolate out of it.

item.content:encoded:
Four seconds. That’s how long it took for SPD Officer Ian Birk to gun down John T. Williams in broad daylight last August 30, as evidenced in this dashboard video that was ordered released by a judge last month. This week, the inquest into this shooting began at the King County Courthouse. Since I’ve posted this video on Facebook and Twitter and even put out this open call to the mayor, we’ve been getting hit up by folks asking how they can take action.

First and foremost: stay posted on all the updates surrounding this case on our local news outlets, particularly independent sources such as The Stranger. Second, there’s been a resurgence of community forums and workshops addressing police violence. Next Monday morning on Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, prior to the annual MLK rally and march at noon, several workshops will be held at Garfield High School. We encourage folks to hit up End Police Violence, Deportation and Suvelliance Now!, conducted by Lynn Domingo in room 217.

For more info on this workshops and MLK Day events, go here.

item.content:encoded:
Running out of hours/cash to get something for that special someone for the holidays? Or don’t particularly observe nor care about the holidays but are down for some free music? Suffice to say, we’ve got the solution. Click the image above for a free download of Winter Pigeons (Songs To Raise Your Dead Spirits), the four-song debut EP by ::M∆DE::IN::HEIGHTS::, Sabzi‘s new project in collaboration with vocalist Kelsey. As Sabzi wrote on townfo.lk,

a little while ago my friend Kelsey and I started talking about forming a group together and making some music. last week it finally happened for really real sugar hill mint’n'dill when we got together in SEA and knocked out a little EP in time to offer it to you all as a seasonal gift.

It describes itself as pop, filth, and New York; we’ll let you decipher the rest on your own. (NB: Definitely keep the ::M∆DE::IN::HEIGHTS:: tumblr handy as you listen along.) Enjoy, and do let us know what you think.

item.content:encoded:
Jokes for days and impeccable styles.

Weather’s been acting crazy lately, huh? Hail, thunder, lightening… and we know why. A force of nature is imminently descending upon our region. Our hilarious homie Hari Kondabolu, who recently filmed an upcoming Comedy Central Presents special to be debuted in February, will be kicking it (read: headlining shows) in Portland and Seattle this week. We highly, highly recommend Hari live, as he wields a comedic veracity unique to a dude from Queens that holds a Masters in Human Rights from the London School of Economics. (And for those not in the know, Hari’s kid brother is Das Racist‘s hypeman Dapwell; they also perform together as the Untitled Kondabolu Brothers Project back in NYC when they’re not globetrotting.)

Check out the clip below, and rally your friends this weekend to see Hari in action.

item.dc:creator: Hollis
item.description: Thanks to the good people at IHeartBlueScholars (we see you!), we just got hip to these customized quilted Nike Blazers inspired by our cut “Life & Debt.” Mister Danny P, the mastermind behind these here kicks, explains: “Life and Debt” is one of my favorite tracks from Blue Scholars. I listened to this song EVERYDAY [...]
item.content:encoded:
Thanks to the good people at IHeartBlueScholars (we see you!), we just got hip to these customized quilted Nike Blazers inspired by our cut “Life & Debt.”  Mister Danny P, the mastermind behind these here kicks, explains:

“Life and Debt” is one of my favorite tracks from Blue Scholars. I listened to this song EVERYDAY for two years when I was away at college. Although it was a love song, the melody put my soul at peace during my rough two years at college, so I wanted a pair that incorporated the words “Life” and “Debt.”

Check out more work by FalseQuest, whose designs across the board are clean and subtly subversive.

And a shoutout to the documentary Life & Debt (Stephanie Black, 2001), which examines Jamaica’s neocolonial economic quandary at the mercy of international lending. Watch it if you haven’t yet, and go fight globalization by supporting local artisans and getting your kicks customized using our song titles.

(Yes, we know Nike is a globalization-benefitting multinational corporation. And so is the supplier of the computer you’re reading this blog post on.)

item.title: Blue Scholars’ Final 2010 Show in Seattle – Tonight at The Crocodile
item.dc:creator: bluescholars
item.description: Our last show of 2010. Back home in Seattle.
item.content:encoded:
Tonight, we’re playing our last show of 2010 back home in Seattle at The Stranger & Redhook’s Rad Winter Party at The Crocodile. Saba’s on a plane right now en route from NYC, where he was just kicking it with Khingz (townbiz). I’m chillin, waiting for the Apple Cup to start, and semi-rehearsing the new new songs we’re debuting tonight.

We announced the show only on our Facebook and Twitter accounts earlier this week and less than a day later, the show was sold out. So don’t get assed out on the next short-notice announcement and make sure you “like” and “follow” us on those things. And if you “don’t do the social network thing,” then be prepared to be the last to know about things like this show in the future!

I got a feeling that tonight’s gonna be a good night (no Will.I.Am). Everybody gets free swag and two drink tickets at the door. Everybody. We’ll be playing some new material from our upcoming album, Cinemetropolis, for the first time onstage. Lastly, tonight also marks the very last time we’ll play a 21+ venue with no 90s babies (legally) in attendance. That’s right yall. Starting January 1, 2011 there will be 90s babies all up in your bar. So to all the 60s, 70s and 80s babies in the building (or before), let’s close out 2010 and celebrate our elder status like we used to. And still do. See you all tonight.

item.title: N30: A Personal History by Geo
item.dc:creator: bluescholars
item.description: N30: A personal history by Geo/Prometheus Brown
item.content:encoded:
I celebrate November 30th for hella reasons.

First and foremost, everywhere Filipinos and real friends of Filipinos are, you’ll find people celebrating the anniversary of revolutionary leader Andres Bonifacio’s birthday (1863). For this reason, on this day in 1964, the national democratic youth organization Kabataang Makabayan was founded at the University of the Philippines, relaunching a movement that saw itself as a continuation of Bonifacio’s unfinished revolution to get the Philippines free from foreign domination.

In 1999, the first day of the World Trade Organization Minesterial Conference drew 50,000 protesters to downtown Seattle – an experience I witnessed firsthand and rapped about on our song 50K Deep. It was the first protest I ever attended, and none have matched that feeling since. So, for me, the “Battle in Seattle” is like the Illmatic of protests. An epic beginning to an era where the follow-ups paled in comparison in the short term but permanently changed the game in the long run.

Blue Scholars “50K Deep” (Bayani, 2007)

In 2002, Anakbayan Seattle, the first overseas chapter of the Philippines-based youth and student organization, was founded. Still riding off that WTO high, jarred by the increasingly hostile post-9/11 political climate, and beginning to see the threads between our homeland and our exiled communities, I joined AB206.

Blue Scholars was founded that same year a few months earlier. Alternating between mobilizations and meetings on one hand and making music on the other, I soon realized that I wasn’t just in some local organization, but part of a mass of people all working towards the same goal. And that there were others doing similar work, such as my brothers Kiwi and Bambu. In fact, Blue Scholars and Native Guns played their first Seattle show together at AB206′s first anniversary show on November 30, 2004. You can hear N30 all over this track:

Native Guns f/ Prometheus Brown “Agitation Propaganda” (Stray Bullets Vol. 2, 2006)

So November 30 is where it all intersects for me: the movement, the music, the fire–literally. We played a show at Holy Names Academy on November 30, 2007 and the speakers caught on fire, the first and only time that’s ever happened.

Now, it’s November 30, 2010 and it’s only fitting that the final day of writing and recording for our next album, Cinemetropolis, lands on this very day. It wasn’t planned this way but weather, work and scheduling made it happen. Or maybe I subconsciously wanted to complete recording on a day of reflection and waited til today. Whatever the case, I’m ready now. N30 for life.
